JUDGE channel — I. Descriptives & response processes

Implicit personality theory in 12 LLMs, read as a rating instrument

ecb

2026-07-23

What this data is, and the stance I take on it

The JUDGE channel (rgb’s tom_likely) asks each model, for every ordered pair of 523 person-descriptive adjectives (i, j), “how strongly would a person described as i also be j?” and reads the answer as an expected rating on a 1–7 Likert scale from the full log-prob distribution over the rating tokens (not the argmax). Each model therefore produces a 523 × 523 matrix B of conditional-endorsement ratings (row-conditioned, not symmetric, diagonal not collected), plus a matching matrix Hent of the Shannon entropy of each rating distribution — a per-judgment uncertainty.

rgb’s own analyses of this data (W15–W16) are geometric and mechanistic: the read/write dissociation, a Helmholtz–Hodge decomposition of the asymmetry, factor congruence to the human 525-PDA. This report series takes the psychometric view the geometry brackets: if we treat these judgments as measurements, are they sound? The unit I adopt (per ecb’s steer) is models as raters — 12 judges rating the same 273,006 ordered pairs. (This reanalysis is built on rgb’s full 7-category raw distributions, judge_dists_full, complete for all 12 cohort models as of 2026-07-20. Earlier versions of these reports used a 12-model EV-only release; the raw distributions supersede it — see the caveat below.) Reliability, validity and response-process questions all follow from the models-as-raters frame.

This first report is the descriptive floor: how does each rater use the scale? Everything downstream (what to do about asymmetry; whether the raters agree; whether the structure is interpretable) is conditioned by the response processes documented here.

Data provenance, stated once — and it shapes the method here. This reanalysis works from the full 7-category rating distributions dists (523×523×7 per model), from which I recompute B (the expected rating) and Hent (the entropy) in float64 so the two moments are internally consistent (the entropy envelope of §1B is respected by construction). These raw distributions supersede the earlier EV-only release, whose bf16 numerics had drifted (mean |ΔEV| 0.02–0.09, with bimodal cells’ EV flipping by up to ~4). Because §§1–5 are framed on the two moments (B, Hent) — the summary a rater’s location and decisiveness are captured by — I keep that framing throughout for continuity and because it is the right altitude for the response-style story; the spread index (§1B) places each judgment’s entropy between the minimum and maximum attainable at its mean, a mean-detrended proxy for how diffuse the underlying distribution is. But two moments cannot see shape (an EV of 4 from “all mass on 4” and from “half on 1, half on 7” are opposite response processes that round identically), and now we can: §6 uses the full 523² raw distributions to give the honest category usage, floor/ceiling, and a shape census — and it corrects the earlier medoid-based verdict that the two-moment proxy was faithful for 10/12 models. Phi4, Aya and FalconMamba are not summarized by EV alone; the earlier error was one of metric (reading faithfulness off strict bimodality) rather than the medoid sample, which in fact tracked off-mode mass reasonably well.

summ <- read_csv_("model_summary.csv") %>% as_tibble() %>%
  mutate(display = factor(display, levels = disp_ord))
marg <- read_csv_("marginals.csv") %>% as_tibble()
dir_ev <- fread_gz("dir_ev.csv.gz")     # i,j, <12 models>  (273006 directional EVs)
dir_h  <- fread_gz("dir_hent.csv.gz")
# long form for distributional plots
ev_long <- melt(dir_ev, id.vars = c("i","j"), variable.name = "model", value.name = "ev")
ev_long[, display := factor(DISPLAY[as.character(model)], levels = disp_ord)]
ev_long[, family  := FAMILY[as.character(model)]]
h_long <- melt(dir_h, id.vars = c("i","j"), variable.name = "model", value.name = "hent")

1. Scale usage: some raters never leave the middle

The single most consequential descriptive fact is that the 12 models do not use the 1–7 scale in remotely the same way. The table sorts by mean rating (leniency); note especially the spread column (ev_sd) and the EV tail fractions (share of judgments with an expected rating in each band).

tab <- summ %>% arrange(ev_mean) %>%
  transmute(Model = display, Family = family, `Params (B)` = params_b,
            `Mean` = round(ev_mean,2), `SD` = round(ev_sd,2),
            `Skew` = round(ev_skew,2), `Excess kurt.` = round(ev_kurtosis,2),
            `% ≤2` = round(100*frac_le2,1), `% 3–5` = round(100*frac_mid_3to5,1),
            `% ≥6` = round(100*frac_ge6,1))
knitr::kable(tab, caption = "Per-rater location, spread and tail usage of the 1–7 scale.")

1A. The distribution of the expected rating

Rather than round B into pseudo-categories, plot its actual distribution per rater — the density of the expected-rating statistic itself. This shows leniency (location) and range restriction (spread) directly and honestly.

ggplot(ev_long, aes(ev)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density), fill = family), bins = 60) +
  facet_wrap(~display, ncol = 4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = FAM_PAL, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:7, limits = c(1,7)) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of the expected rating B, per rater",
       x = "expected rating (1–7)", y = "density") +
  theme_judge()

Read as a response-style census:

  • Range-restricted / central responders. Llama3.2-3B’s expected ratings collapse onto a narrow 4–5 band (SD = 0.46) — whatever the pair, the answer is “middling”. FalconMamba-7B is similarly compressed (SD = 0.75) but for a different reason: §3/§6 show it sits near the uniform entropy ceiling (broad distributions whose means land mid-scale), not a confident middle.
  • Full-range responders with ceiling/floor mass. Aya-expanse-8B and Phi4-mini spread expected ratings across the whole scale with heavy mass toward the ceiling (SD ≈ 1.7–1.9) — §6 shows these are among the models whose raw distributions are genuinely diffuse (real mass at both ends), not just wide-ranging means.
  • Gemma family is central-to-high and, on the raw data (§6), the most concentrated (Gemma-4-31B is the sharpest rater in the cohort).
  • Qwen family sits modal around 3–4 (the most parsimonious raters, mean 3.6–3.7) with intermediate spread.

1B. Spread index: are the underlying distributions concentrated or diffuse?

The expected rating hides the shape of the distribution it came from. Since we also hold each judgment’s entropy, we can recover how concentrated the underlying rating distribution is, detrended for its mean — the raw entropy mechanically falls near the scale ends, so a bare entropy comparison confounds concentration with leniency. The spread index places each judgment’s entropy between the minimum and maximum entropy attainable at its mean (0 = as concentrated as any distribution with that mean can be; 1 = maximally diffuse). It is the closest honest proxy to the raw response shape.

ev_long[, spread := spread_index(ev, h_long$hent)]
sp_summ <- ev_long[, .(mean_spread = mean(spread, na.rm = TRUE)), by = display]
ggplot(ev_long[!is.na(spread)][sample(.N, 120000)], aes(spread, y = display, fill = after_stat(x))) +
  ggridges::geom_density_ridges_gradient(scale = 2.2, rel_min_height = 0.01, linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "spread", option = "C") +
  labs(title = "Spread index by rater (mean-detrended concentration of the rating distribution)",
       subtitle = "left = concentrated / decisive · right = diffuse / hedged",
       x = "spread index", y = NULL) +
  theme_judge() + theme(legend.position = "right")

knitr::kable(
  sp_summ %>% arrange(mean_spread) %>% transmute(Model = display, `Mean spread` = round(mean_spread,3)),
  caption = "Mean spread index per rater — a mean-independent response-style axis.")
Mean spread index per rater — a mean-independent response-style axis.
Model Mean spread
Gemma-4-31B 0.045
Gemma3-27B 0.063
Gemma3-12B 0.085
Gemma3-4B 0.108
Qwen2.5-32B 0.167
Qwen2.5-7B 0.367
Llama3.2-3B 0.512
Qwen2.5-3B 0.532
Aya-expanse-8B 0.568
Llama3.1-8B 0.652
FalconMamba-7B 0.870
Phi4-mini-3.8B 0.935

This re-sorts the cohort on a genuinely different axis than leniency or SD: the Gemma family produces the most concentrated underlying distributions (mean spread 0.05–0.11, Gemma-4-31B the sharpest — it commits to sharp judgments) while Phi4-mini and FalconMamba-7B are the most diffuse (0.87–0.94 — their judgments are broad even where the expected rating is mid-scale). Note this is not the same as the SD of B: a rater can produce a wide range of expected ratings out of individually diffuse distributions (Phi4) or a narrow range out of sharp ones. Concentration and differentiation are distinct response-style dimensions — the point §4 formalizes.

This is exactly the heterogeneity that makes cross-model magnitude comparison unsafe (rgb’s calibration caveat) — but stated in response-style terms it is sharper: these are different rating styles, not just different means. Range restriction limits how much differentiated information a rater can carry (it caps the achievable between-pair variance) — though, importantly, Report III shows it does not make these raters disagree with the crowd: a flat rater is low-information, not noisy.

2. Location and spread are only loosely coupled

ggplot(summ, aes(ev_mean, ev_sd, colour = family, label = display)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(size = 3, max.overlaps = 20, seed = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = FAM_PAL, name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Rater leniency (mean) vs differentiation (SD)",
       x = "mean rating (leniency →)", y = "SD of ratings (differentiation →)") +
  theme_judge()

Leniency (mean 3.64 → 4.83) and differentiation (SD 0.46 → 1.95) vary independently: Llama3.2-3B is lenient but flat (high mean, tiny SD — it agrees warmly with almost everything), whereas Aya is lenient and spread. A high mean does not buy you usable variance. For the measurement, differentiation (SD) is the resource — a rater with SD 0.47 can encode at most a sliver of true between-pair signal.

3. Decisiveness: the entropy channel is a second, partly independent axis

Each judgment carries an entropy. Averaged per rater, this is a decisiveness index that is not the same thing as scale spread.

ggplot(h_long, aes(x = factor(DISPLAY[as.character(model)], levels = disp_ord), y = hent,
                   fill = FAMILY[as.character(model)])) +
  geom_violin(scale = "width", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = FAM_PAL, name = NULL) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Per-judgment entropy (uncertainty) by rater",
       x = NULL, y = "Shannon entropy of the 1–7 rating distribution (nats)") +
  theme_judge()

# entropy as a function of the rating level: the response-process signature
set.seed(1)
samp <- ev_long[sample(.N, 60000)][, .(i,j,model,ev)]
samp <- merge(samp, h_long[, .(i,j,model,hent)], by = c("i","j","model"))
samp[, display := factor(DISPLAY[as.character(model)], levels = disp_ord)]
ggplot(samp, aes(ev, hent)) +
  geom_hex(bins = 40) + scale_fill_viridis_c(trans = "log10", name = "pairs") +
  facet_wrap(~display, ncol = 4, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Entropy vs expected rating — the graded-in-the-middle signature",
       x = "expected rating", y = "entropy") +
  theme_judge() + theme(legend.position = "right")

Two things:

  1. The inverted-U (entropy peaks at mid-scale, collapses at the extremes) is present for the discriminating raters — a sensible response process: the model is certain when it judges a pair clearly (dis)similar and hedges in between.
  2. The non-responsive raters break it. FalconMamba-7B sits at entropy ≈ 1.66 nats almost everywhere (near the log(7)=1.95 uniform ceiling) — it is maximally uncertain on nearly every pair. Llama3.2-3B is similar in effect (mean ≈ 1.09 nats and essentially never decisive: only 0.002% of its judgments have entropy < 0.1, versus 49–67% for the Gemma family). Their narrow EV in §1 is now explained: they are not compressing a confident signal, they are reporting near-flat distributions whose means happen to sit mid-scale. (Note the discriminating raters Phi4-mini and Llama3.1-8B also carry high entropy, ≈ 1.26 nats, but do differentiate — a wide-then-hedged style, not non-response; §6 confirms Phi4 carries real off-mode mass.)

4. A response-process typology: two kinds of “uncertain”

Crossing scale differentiation (SD of B) against concentration (mean spread index, §1B — the mean-detrended decisiveness) separates raters that look similar on either axis alone.

typ <- summ %>% left_join(sp_summ, by = "display")
ggplot(typ, aes(mean_spread, ev_sd, colour = family, label = display)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(size = 3, max.overlaps = 20, seed = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = FAM_PAL, name = NULL) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = median(typ$mean_spread), linetype = 3, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = median(typ$ev_sd), linetype = 3, colour = "grey60") +
  labs(title = "Response-process typology",
       subtitle = "up-left = confident differentiator · down-right = diffuse non-discriminator",
       x = "mean spread index (← concentrated/decisive | diffuse →)",
       y = "SD of expected ratings (↑ differentiated)") +
  theme_judge()

  • Confident differentiators (low spread, high SD): the Gemma family, esp. Gemma-4-31B/Gemma3-27B. They commit to sharp, well-separated judgments — §6 confirms they are ≥99% unimodal on the raw data.
  • Diffuse non-discriminators (high spread, low SD): FalconMamba-7B most clearly — broad distributions and little between-pair signal. Llama3.2-3B is the low-SD / low-information corner but only mid-spread. (§6 shows FalconMamba’s breadth is a diffuse, digit-prior distribution (~78% off-mode mass but ~90% unimodal), not a bimodal one — the spread index cannot see that difference.)
  • Spread-but-hedging (high spread, high SD): Aya, Phi4-mini — they use the whole scale yet keep each individual distribution diffuse. (§6, on the full raw distributions, shows these two are where the two-moment proxy fails: Phi4 puts ≥0.25 off-mode mass in 56% of cells and Aya in 26%, and Aya makes genuine no-OR-yes mixtures in ~15% of judgments — invisible to EV+entropy.)

This typology is the load-bearing setup for reliability — but with a twist that Report III makes precise and that is easy to get wrong: a diffuse non-discriminator carries little differentiated information (its between-pair variance is small), yet it still agrees with the consensus and does not inject noise (its judgments are a smooth, prevalence-tracking, compressed image of the crowd’s). So the flat raters are low-information, not low-quality; the raters that actually pull away from the consensus turn out to be the high-variance idiosyncratic models, not the flat ones. Weighting/trimming therefore buys much less than the typology first suggests (Report III §3, Report V).

5. Marginal structure: base rates (prevalence) and anchor generosity

Because the diagonal (self-pairs) was not collected, each rater’s matrix has two informative margins:

  • column mean = how strongly adjective j is ascribed given any anchor — a base rate / prevalence (“Awake”, “Normal” are ascribed to almost anyone).
  • row mean = how generously anchor i ascribes other traits — anchor-level acquiescence.
mm <- marg %>% mutate(display = factor(DISPLAY[model], levels = disp_ord))
ggplot(mm, aes(col_mean, fill = FAMILY[model])) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40) + facet_wrap(~display, ncol = 4, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = FAM_PAL, guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Target base-rate (column-mean) distribution per rater",
       x = "mean ascription of a target across all anchors (prevalence)", y = "count") +
  theme_judge()

cohort_prev <- mm %>% group_by(adjective) %>% summarise(prev = mean(col_mean)) %>%
  arrange(desc(prev))
knitr::kable(
  bind_cols(
    cohort_prev %>% slice_head(n = 12) %>% transmute(`Most universally ascribed` = adjective, `μ` = round(prev,2)),
    cohort_prev %>% slice_tail(n = 12) %>% arrange(prev) %>% transmute(`Least ascribed` = adjective, ` μ` = round(prev,2))
  ), caption = "Cohort-mean target base rates (prevalence marginals).")

The prevalence marginal is large and structured — and it is precisely what a marginal-free human correlation matrix does not contain, which is why the reliability and validity reports double-center (strip additive row/column marginals) before treating B as a similarity. It is also the primary axis of the asymmetry (Report II).

6. The full raw distributions: what the two moments actually hide

Sections 1–5 read each judgment through its two moments (B, Hent). We now hold the full 523×523×7 rating distributions for all 12 cohort raters, so we can replace the proxy with ground truth over the entire pair space — honest category usage, floor and ceiling mass, and a distribution-shape census — and settle, at cohort scale, what the two moments summarize well and what they miss.

This corrects an earlier verdict — but not in the way the internal handoff note anticipated, and the difference is itself the finding. A prior version of this section used a 35-adjective facet-medoid sample and concluded the (EV, entropy) proxy was “faithful for 10/12 models.” The natural hypothesis was that medoids — facet exemplars, i.e. central prototypical cases — under-represent the diffuse judgments in the messy middle of the 523² space, so the full set would look far more spread. The data only partly bears that out (§6.1), and the real error turns out to be one of metric, not sample (§6.3).

shp  <- read_csv_("full_shape.csv") %>% as_tibble() %>%
  mutate(display = factor(DISPLAY[model], levels = disp_ord))
cm   <- read_csv_("full_catmass.csv") %>% as_tibble() %>%
  mutate(display = factor(display, levels = disp_ord), cat = factor(cat))

6.1 The medoid sample was a reasonable proxy for off-mode mass

Recomputing rgb’s off-mode-mass metric (fraction of off-diagonal cells that place ≥ 0.25 probability ≥ 2 categories away from the modal rating) on the 35-medoid sample vs the full 523² set:

offmode_frac <- function(P) {           # P: matrix rows = 7-cat pmfs
  m <- max.col(P, ties.method = "first")
  far <- abs(col(P) - m) >= 2
  mean(rowSums(P * far) >= 0.25)
}
md <- fread_gz("medoids_dists.csv.gz"); pcols <- paste0("p", 1:7)
md_off <- md[model %in% MODELS, .(medoid = offmode_frac(as.matrix(.SD))),
             by = model, .SDcols = pcols]
comp <- shp %>% transmute(model, full = offmode_frac) %>%
  left_join(md_off, by = "model") %>%
  transmute(Model = DISPLAY[model],
            `Off-mode % (35-medoid)` = round(100*medoid,1),
            `Off-mode % (full 523²)` = round(100*full,1),
            `Δ` = round(100*(full-medoid),1)) %>%
  arrange(desc(`Off-mode % (full 523²)`))
knitr::kable(comp, caption = "rgb's off-mode-mass metric, medoid sample vs full 523². The medoids track it well; the drift is a few points (the Llamas roughly double off a low base).")
rgb’s off-mode-mass metric, medoid sample vs full 523². The medoids track it well; the drift is a few points (the Llamas roughly double off a low base).
Model Off-mode % (35-medoid) Off-mode % (full 523²) Δ

Phi4-mini-3.8B 50.5 56.1 5.6
Aya-expanse-8B 26.6 26.2 -0.4
Llama3.1-8B 4.8 10.4 5.6
Qwen2.5-3B 6.7 7.6 0.8

Qwen2.5-7B 3.0 4.4 1.4

Contrary to the “medoids badly under-represent spread” hypothesis, the medoid sample tracked off-mode mass remarkably well: FalconMamba reads 78.8% on the medoids vs 78.3% on the full set, Phi4 50.5% vs 56.1%, Aya 26.6% vs 26.2%. The exemplars drift slightly low only for the Llamas (which roughly double, 2→7% and 5→10%, off small bases) but the ranking and the qualitative story are preserved. So the medoid sample was not the problem. The blanket “faithful for 10/12” verdict is nonetheless wrong for FalconMamba, Phi4 and Aya — and §6.3 shows why the earlier analysis missed it: it read faithfulness off strict bimodality alone, when the operative failure is off-mode mass.

6.2 True category usage (the honest version of §1), cohort-wide

Actual mean probability mass per rating category over all 273,006 off-diagonal judgments — no rounding, no proxy:

ggplot(cm, aes(cat, mean_mass, fill = cat)) +
  geom_col() + facet_wrap(~display, ncol = 3) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "RdYlBu", direction = -1, guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "True mean category mass (full 523², 12 raters)",
       x = "rating category 1–7", y = "mean probability") + theme_judge()

The location story of §1 holds (Qwen is floor-leaning, Gemma central-to-high, Llama3.2 hugs 4–5), but the honest picture also shows how much end-mass Aya and Phi4 carry (mass on category 1 ≈ 0.18 / 0.15; on category 7 ≈ 0.39 / 0.37) — the raw signature of diffuse, often U-shaped judgments that no expected rating can convey.

6.3 Two different questions: off-mode mass vs genuine bimodality

“Diffuse” and “bimodal” are not the same claim, and the full data lets us separate them — which resolves what the off-mode metric can and can’t say:

  • Off-mode mass (rgb’s metric, §6.1): how much probability sits ≥ 2 categories from the mode. High = the EV is a poor summary, but the distribution could be broad-unimodal.
  • Prominence bimodality (shape_class, requiring a real valley < 0.6× the smaller of two peaks ≥ 0.15): a genuine two-mode “no OR yes” semantic mixture, distinguished from a digit-notch (a dip at a dispreferred digit 2/6 — a rating-channel artifact, echoing the Llama-2 category-2 suppression in the soft-evidence track).
knitr::kable(
  shp %>% arrange(desc(semantic)) %>%
    transmute(Model = DISPLAY[model],
              `Off-mode %` = round(100*offmode_frac,1),
              `unimodal %` = round(100*unimodal,1),
              `semantic %` = round(100*semantic,1),
              `digit-notch %` = round(100*`digit-notch`,1),
              `adjacent %` = round(100*adjacent,1)),
  caption = "Off-mode mass vs a strict shape census over all 523². High off-mode need NOT mean bimodal.")

The census sharpens §6.1 into the real finding — three different ways to be “off-mode,” only one of them genuine bimodality:

  1. FalconMamba has the most off-mode mass (78%) yet is not bimodal — 90% unimodal, with the off-mode share split between a small digit-notch component (6.3% — it under-uses digits 2 and 6 as the mode) and a broad, near-uniform spread (its mean entropy is 1.66 nats, ~85% of the log(7) ceiling). This is the flat rater of §§1,3 seen from the distribution side: diffuse with a digit prior, not a two-mode judgment. It is the sharpest example of why the off-mode flag must not be read as bimodality.
  2. Phi4 is diffuse but not strongly bimodal. Despite 56% off-mode mass it is 93% unimodal — its judgments are broad, flat-topped (rgb’s “commit-vs-hedge” modes), not clean two-mode mixtures. Its EV genuinely mis-summarizes it, but the shape is spread, not split.
  3. Aya is the one genuinely bimodal rater — 15% semantic mixtures (empty-middle “almost certainly no, but sometimes yes” distributions), on top of its 26% off-mode mass. This is the case the two moments materially misread as a mid/high mean.
  4. The Gemma family (incl. the ultra-sharp Gemma-4-31B), Qwen2.5-32B and Llama3.1-8B are ≥ 98% unimodal — for them EV + entropy lose essentially nothing, off-mode mass and all.
  5. Digit-2/6 suppression is real but minor, running through FalconMamba (6.3%), the Qwen family (Qwen2.5-7B 4.4% digit-notch) and Aya (8%) — a rating-channel artifact to keep in mind, not substantive structure.
ex <- read_csv_("full_examples.csv") %>% as_tibble()
exl <- ex %>%
  mutate(who = sprintf("%s: %s→%s  (EV=%.1f, %s)", display, adj_i, adj_j, ev, shape)) %>%
  select(who, shape, p1:p7) %>%
  pivot_longer(p1:p7, names_to = "cat", values_to = "p") %>%
  mutate(cat = as.integer(sub("p", "", cat)),
         who = factor(who, levels = unique(who)))
ggplot(exl, aes(factor(cat), p, fill = shape)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) + facet_wrap(~who, ncol = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(semantic = "#8172B3", unimodal = "#DD8452")) +
  labs(title = "Same expected rating, opposite response process",
       subtitle = "EV+entropy (and the spread index) cannot tell these apart; only the raw distribution can",
       x = "rating category", y = "probability") + theme_judge()

Each Phi4/Aya semantic mixture is paired with a matched-EV unimodal judgment from the sharp Gemma3-27B: identical expected rating, opposite underlying process — the exact failure mode the two-moment summary cannot see.

6.4 Verdict — and what it enables

The full distributions correct the medoid-era conclusion: the (EV, entropy) summary is adequate for 9 of the 12 raters (the Gemmas, both Llamas, all three Qwens) but not for FalconMamba, Phi4 or Aya — and, tellingly, it fails on all three differently: FalconMamba is diffuse-with-a-digit-prior, Phi4 broad-unimodal, Aya genuinely bimodal. The spread index of §1B did flag all three as diffuse — it was doing its job — but a two-moment index cannot tell those three shapes apart, and the distinction matters for what a judgment means. The earlier verdict erred not because the 35-medoid sample was unrepresentative (§6.1 shows it tracked off-mode mass well) but because it certified faithfulness off strict bimodality alone — and FalconMamba/Phi4, ~90% unimodal yet 78%/56% off-mode, slip exactly through that gap. The lesson is methodological as much as empirical: pick the diffuseness metric that matches the question.

Two implications:

  • The under-sold flat rater. FalconMamba’s graded, near-uniform mass is precisely what a mean+entropy summary throws away — yet rgb reports its distributional readout carries the cohort’s strongest correspondence to the human 525-PDA structure (EV r ≈ 0.73). The model the EV-only storage under-sold most is the one whose full distribution matters most — a direct argument for keeping the raw 7-way data.
  • The full 7-way distributions open a soft-evidence treatment (bridging ecb’s earlier soft-evidence IRT work): distributional similarity (e.g. earth-mover distance between two judgment distributions) as an alternative to EV-cosine, and genuine confidence weighting from real distributions rather than an entropy proxy — most valuable exactly for the three raters (FalconMamba, Aya, Phi4) the moments fail on.

7. Reading the raw distributions as response processes

§6 used the full distributions to audit the two-moment summary. But the distributions carry response-process information the moments cannot even pose a question about: at a fixed expected rating, how does a model arrive there — does it slide a graded peak, split its mass, sit on a fixed digit habit, or flip a coin? This section reads the raw (523×523×7) tensors on their own terms. (Products from dist_processes.py.)

7.1 The response-process signature: same expected rating, different process

Fix the expected rating and look at the shape. Below, for each rater, is the mean 7-category distribution of its judgments as a function of their expected rating (columns = EV bins, rows = rating category, brightness = mean probability). A purely graded responder would trace a thin bright band along the diagonal (peak follows the EV); anything off the diagonal is a response process the EV hides.

sig <- read_csv_("proc_signature.csv") %>% as_tibble() %>%
  mutate(display = factor(display, levels = disp_ord))
ggplot(sig, aes(ev_bin, cat, fill = mean_mass)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "white", linetype = 3, linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~display, ncol = 3) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "mean prob.", option = "C") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:7) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:7, limits = c(1, 7)) +
  labs(title = "Response-process signature: rating distribution vs expected rating, per rater",
       subtitle = "dotted line = pure graded response (peak on the diagonal); off-diagonal mass is what EV hides",
       x = "expected rating (EV bin)", y = "rating category (1–7)") +
  theme_judge() + theme(legend.position = "right")

Five distinct processes are legible at a glance, and they are not orderable on one axis:

  • Graded slide — the Gemma family (esp. Gemma3-27B/Gemma-4-31B) hugs the diagonal tightly: the distribution is a single sharp peak that tracks the expected rating almost perfectly. At EV ≈ 4 they put ~0.98 mass on category 4. This is the ideal graded response.
  • Endpoint fork — Aya keeps visible mass at categories 1 and 7 across the whole EV range: at a mid-scale expected rating it is not sitting at 4, it is splitting between “no” and “yes”. The diagonal is there but a persistent two-band fork rides on top of it.
  • Fixed digit habit — FalconMamba shows near-horizontal bands at categories 1/3/4/5 that barely move with EV: the shape is a stock digit prior, not a response to the pair (§7.2 makes this precise). Llama3.2-3B is the compact version — a fixed blob at 4–5.
  • Broad diffuse — Phi4-mini traces the diagonal but fat, with a persistent secondary shoulder around 6: it commits softly and hedges wide.

The Gemmas and FalconMamba have the same EV range yet opposite signatures — a graded slide vs a fixed habit. No summary of location and spread can separate those; the signature requires the raw distribution.

7.2 A rater’s rating variability, decomposed: content vs hedge

The signature suggests a sharper, information-theoretic question. A rater’s total rating variability is H(marginal) — the entropy of its category usage pooled over all pairs. That splits exactly into two response-process pieces:

\[H(\text{marginal}) \;=\; \underbrace{I(\text{pair};\text{rating})}_{\text{content: how much the pair drives the rating}} \;+\; \underbrace{\overline{H(\text{rating}\mid\text{pair})}}_{\text{hedge: mean within-judgment entropy}}\]

The first term is the mutual information the adjective pair carries about the rating — the part of a rater’s output that is about the question. The second is its mean per-judgment entropy — fixed hedging that is the same whatever the pair. mean Hent (the decisiveness of §3) is only the second term; the raw distributions give us the first.

con <- read_csv_("proc_content.csv") %>% as_tibble() %>%
  mutate(display = factor(display, levels = disp_ord))
cl <- con %>%
  transmute(display, content_frac,
            `content (MI)` = MI_nats, `hedge (mean within-entropy)` = mean_within_entropy) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(`content (MI)`, `hedge (mean within-entropy)`),
               names_to = "component", values_to = "nats") %>%
  mutate(display = factor(display, levels = con$display[order(con$content_frac)]))
ggplot(cl, aes(nats, display, fill = component)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("content (MI)" = "#4C72B0",
                               "hedge (mean within-entropy)" = "#DD8452"), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "A rater's total rating entropy, split into content vs hedge",
       subtitle = "bar length = H(marginal); blue = mutual information the pair carries about the rating",
       x = "nats", y = NULL) + theme_judge()

knitr::kable(
  con %>% arrange(desc(content_frac)) %>%
    transmute(Model = display, `H(marginal)` = round(H_marginal, 2),
              `MI (content)` = round(MI_nats, 2), `mean Hent (hedge)` = round(mean_within_entropy, 2),
              `content %` = round(100 * content_frac, 1)),
  caption = "The rating-variability budget. 'content %' = fraction of a rater's rating entropy that is about the pair.")
The rating-variability budget. ‘content %’ = fraction of a rater’s rating entropy that is about the pair.
Model H(marginal) MI (content) mean Hent (hedge) content %
Gemma3-27B 1.67 1.53 0.14 91.5
Gemma-4-31B 1.30 1.19 0.11 91.5
Gemma3-12B 1.59 1.37 0.22 86.3
Gemma3-4B 1.51 1.28 0.23 84.8
Qwen2.5-32B 1.46 1.09 0.37 74.7
Qwen2.5-3B 1.84 0.96 0.88 52.3
Qwen2.5-7B 1.53 0.80 0.74 52.1
Aya-expanse-8B 1.67 0.87 0.80 51.9
Phi4-mini-3.8B 1.75 0.48 1.27 27.6
Llama3.1-8B 1.70 0.44 1.26 26.0
Llama3.2-3B 1.27 0.19 1.09 14.8
FalconMamba-7B 1.79 0.13 1.66 7.5

This reframes what “flat” means, and does so more sharply than the SD of B. FalconMamba has one of the highest total rating entropies in the cohort (H(marginal) ≈ 1.79 nats — it uses the scale widely) — yet only 7.5% of it is content: 92% of its output is a fixed hedge that ignores the pair. Llama3.2-3B is the same story at lower volume (15% content). At the other end the Gemma family and Qwen2.5-32B are 75–92% content — nearly all of their rating variability is about the question. The discriminating-but-diffuse raters sit in between (Phi4 28%, Llama3.1-8B 26%): genuinely responsive, but hedging half their signal away.

So the low-information raters of Report III are low-information distributionally — not because they use a narrow slice of the scale (FalconMamba doesn’t), but because their distributions barely depend on the pair. This is the mutual-information version of the “SD of B” axis, and it is the quantity a soft-evidence model should actually weight by (a high-entropy but low-content judgment deserves little weight — exactly what an inverse-entropy weight gets wrong for FalconMamba).

7.3 What the second mode means: three mechanisms behind “off-mode” mass

When a distribution is multi-modal, the two moments (and even the off-mode-mass flag of §6) can’t say what the second mode is for. Censusing the (lower, higher) mode pair of every genuinely bi-modal cell separates three completely different response processes:

mp <- read_csv_("proc_modepairs.csv") %>% as_tibble()
key <- c("Aya-expanse-8B", "Phi4-mini-3.8B", "FalconMamba-7B", "Qwen2.5-7B")
mpk <- mp %>% filter(display %in% key) %>%
  mutate(display = factor(display, levels = key))
ggplot(mpk, aes(hi, lo, fill = frac)) +
  geom_tile() + facet_wrap(~display, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "frac of\nbimodal cells", option = "D", trans = "sqrt") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:7) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:7) +
  labs(title = "Mode-pair census: which two categories are the modes, in bimodal cells",
       x = "higher mode", y = "lower mode") + theme_judge() + theme(legend.position = "right")

  • No-OR-yes (semantic) — the (1, 7) corner: a genuine “almost certainly not / sometimes yes” mixture. Present but a minority even where it is most common (Aya ~21% of its bimodal cells; Phi4 ~18%).
  • Commit-vs-hedge — Phi4’s signature: its dominant mode pairs are (4, 7) (34%) and (4, 6) (28%) — a hedge mode at the mid-scale and a commit mode at the top, exactly rgb’s reading. This is not “no vs yes”; it is “shrug vs endorse”, and it rides on top of a broadly unimodal shape (which is why Phi4 is 93% unimodal yet 56% off-mode).
  • Digit-notch artifact — Qwen2.5-7B is 82% (1, 3): a mode at 1 and a mode at 3 with the dip at the dispreferred digit 2. FalconMamba’s pairs are (1, 4) and (5, 7) (42% each) — lumps between its preferred digits 1/3/4/5, skipping 2 and 6. These “modes” are a tokenizer prior, not a judgment — the distributional echo of the Llama-2 category-2 suppression from the soft-evidence track.

So a single “bimodality” flag conflates a semantic mixture, a commit/hedge split, and a rating-channel artifact. Only the raw distribution — specifically where the modes sit — tells them apart.

7.4 Coin-flips on ill-posed pairs: where EV is most misleading

The starkest response process is the balanced (1, 7) coin-flip: half the mass on “very unlikely”, half on “very likely”, nothing between. Its expected rating is ≈ 4 — dead neutral — but the process is the opposite of a neutral judgment. These cells are rare (Aya ~3% of judgments; others < 1%) and, tellingly, they cluster on category-orthogonal targets:

ex <- read_csv_("proc_endpoint_examples.csv") %>% as_tibble()
knitr::kable(
  ex %>% filter(display %in% c("Aya-expanse-8B", "Phi4-mini-3.8B", "Qwen2.5-3B")) %>%
    group_by(display) %>% slice_head(n = 3) %>% ungroup() %>%
    transmute(Rater = display, Pair = paste0(adj_i, " → ", adj_j),
              EV = round(ev, 1), `p(1)` = round(p1, 2), `p(7)` = round(p7, 2)),
  caption = "Balanced 1-vs-7 coin-flips. EV reads ‘neutral’; the process is maximal binary uncertainty.")
Balanced 1-vs-7 coin-flips. EV reads ‘neutral’; the process is maximal binary uncertainty.
Rater Pair EV p(1) p(7)
Aya-expanse-8B sentimental → artificial 4.0 0.50 0.50
Aya-expanse-8B determined → artificial 4.0 0.50 0.50
Aya-expanse-8B truthful → good-for-nothing 4.0 0.50 0.50
Phi4-mini-3.8B intelligent → guilty 4.1 0.43 0.43
Phi4-mini-3.8B religious → guilty 4.1 0.43 0.43
Phi4-mini-3.8B superstitious → unattractive 4.0 0.42 0.42
Qwen2.5-3B outstanding → good-for-nothing 4.0 0.50 0.50
Qwen2.5-3B narrow-minded → artificial 4.0 0.49 0.49
Qwen2.5-3B thankful → evil 4.0 0.49 0.49

Phi4’s coin-flips are almost all → guilty (intelligent → guilty, religious → guilty, muscular → guilty, energetic → guilty …): a competence or physical anchor asked “how likely also guilty?” — a moral-category question orthogonal to the anchor. Aya’s and Qwen’s land on → artificial, → good-for-nothing, → evil. The pattern is a genuine response process: faced with an ill-posed, category-mismatched pair, these models flip between the extremes rather than hedge to the middle — so their (1, 7) bimodality is partly the model recognizing that the question does not compose. This is the single case where rounding EV to “4 = neither likely nor unlikely” most badly misreads what happened, and it is invisible without the raw distribution.

7.5 What this adds

Read as response processes, the raw distributions turn “how uncertain is this rater” into “uncertain how”: content vs hedge (§7.2), graded-slide vs endpoint-fork vs fixed-digit (§7.1), semantic mixture vs commit/hedge vs digit artifact (§7.3), and coin-flip-on-ill-posed (§7.4). None of these is recoverable from B and Hent. Two have immediate measurement payoff: (a) content share I(pair;rating)/H(marginal) is the right per-rater information weight (and correctly demotes FalconMamba, which an entropy weight would over-trust), and (b) the mode-pair mechanism tells a soft-evidence model which off-mode mass is signal (semantic) versus nuisance (digit artifact) — a cleaner footing than either the EV-cosine or a raw earth-mover distance.

Takeaways for the measurement program

  1. Scale use is a rater property, not a constant. Leniency, differentiation and decisiveness each vary ~4× across the cohort and are only loosely coupled — three separate response-style nuisances to model, not one calibration knob.
  2. Two raters (Llama3.2-3B, FalconMamba-7B) are range-restricted / low-information. They carry little differentiated signal — but Report III shows they still agree with the consensus and do not harm it, so exclusion is not warranted; the ensemble is robust. (This corrects the tempting “down-weight the flat raters” intuition.)
  3. The entropy channel is real signal — but entropy is the wrong weight. The inverted-U response process is sensible for discriminating raters; where it flattens, the rater is guessing. But §7.2 shows a per-judgment entropy weight over-trusts FalconMamba (high entropy, near-zero content); the right per-rater weight is the content share I(pair;rating)/H(marginal), which the raw distributions give and the two moments do not.
  4. Big additive marginals (prevalence + anchor generosity) must be removed before B is read as a similarity — motivating the symmetrization + double-centering in Reports II–IV.
  5. On the full raw distributions (§6), the two-moment summary is adequate for 9 of the 12 raters but fails for FalconMamba, Phi4 and Aya — correcting the earlier “faithful for 10/12” verdict, which erred by certifying faithfulness off strict bimodality alone (the 35-medoid sample actually tracked off-mode mass fine — FalconMamba 78.8%→78.3%, Phi4 50%→56%). The three failures are different: FalconMamba is diffuse with a digit prior, Phi4 is diffuse but broad-unimodal (56% off-mode, 93% unimodal), while Aya is genuinely bimodal (~15% empty-middle semantic mixtures). The spread index correctly flags all three as diffuse but cannot tell those shapes apart — which is exactly why the full distributions matter, and where a soft-evidence treatment should start. A minor digit-2/6 suppression artifact runs through FalconMamba, the Qwen family and Aya.
  6. Read as response processes (§7), the distributions say “uncertain how”, not just “how uncertain”. (a) A rater’s rating entropy splits into content (mutual information the pair carries about the rating) + hedge (fixed within-judgment entropy): the Gemmas are 75–92% content, while FalconMamba is 7.5% — “flat” is low-content, not low-variability.
    1. Holding EV fixed, the category distribution reveals distinct processes — graded slide (Gemma), endpoint fork (Aya), fixed digit habit (FalconMamba), broad diffuse (Phi4). (c) The location of the second mode separates semantic no-vs-yes from Phi4’s commit-vs-hedge and the Qwen/Falcon digit-notch artifact. (d) Balanced 1-vs-7 coin-flips cluster on category-orthogonal pairs (Phi4 → guilty): the model flips rather than hedges on ill-posed questions, the one place EV ≈ 4 most badly misreads the process. ```
